note: Two passes by the journalist's research agents over newsroom.sgit.ai: the 107 article sources in admin/content/articles/ and the 97 articles imported from sgit.ai that exist only as published markdown (index and graphs pages left out). Every article read by its title, summary and the core idea of its graph; 'in_map' says whether admin/content/map.json already cites it.

articles.title: A book for one reader: a personalised edition of Generation Z Developers, assembled by an agent for one person, and paid for as it is read
articles.why: Plans personalised, metered editions of this book; guides the agents producing editions, not a reader chapter.

articles.title: A browser for one: an iPhone app that only reads my newsroom, why I am building it now, and why I will still pay someone to keep it working
articles.why: Take the story: frustration plus the power to build turns into an app for one person, and 'being able to compile a Linux kernel does not mean I want to' maintain it, the explorer-to-villager handover in daily life.

articles.title: A custom Firefox of my own: the full plan to build one with a governed agent hive, for the laptop and the iPad, and how Mozilla could sell me the part I do not want to do, which is keeping it working
articles.why: Take the number: a Firefox fork must be rebased 26 times a year on two codebases, the concrete cost of maintenance that explorers underestimate; and the 'least invasive layer first' habit.

articles.title: A directory of people and their keys: pki.sgit.ai for the people I work with, verified by me first, then by each other, and a link that only counts when it goes both ways
articles.why: sgit PKI product brief, niche.

articles.title: A link to a persona: send people to the newsroom as someone, not as nobody
articles.why: newsroom persona link feature

articles.title: A Mac of the agent's own: a business plan for agent desktops, what Apple's licence allows, and three behaviour policies
articles.why: business plan for agent Macs

articles.title: A meter in the browser: a penny a page, a history you keep, and a site that picks for you
articles.why: reading meter experiment design

articles.title: A minimal viable browser: why Firefox is the one that can build it, and what it would take
articles.why: Take the line 'an agent cannot leak what its browser cannot reach' and the browser as the biggest attack surface we run; answers the Xcode and web-proxies outlines.

articles.title: A model in the tab: Chrome now ships an LLM to capable desktops, and it is the hardest piece of the client-side puzzle
articles.why: Take the fact: since Chrome 148 any page can prompt Gemini Nano on the reader's own device, a free model for student projects. Partly fills the costs gap.

articles.title: A personal agent that keeps your secrets: the 2026 agents read through behaviour policy and encryption, and a privacy-first design on vaults, enclaves and the browser
articles.why: Background for the agents: the 2026 personal-agent products read for barriers and data sovereignty.

articles.title: A policy beside the prompt: a proposal that every agent takes a behaviour policy as an input, with enforcement and liability attached, and why aviation and payments say the vendors should want it
articles.why: Take the aviation number (1995 accident rate would mean about a hundred fatal accidents a year instead of twelve) and payments liability as the story of why safety follows when rule, liability and business model align.

articles.title: A policy for every skill: Sean Turner's natural-language control for agent skills, the behaviour policy behind it, and using models to need them less
articles.why: Take Sean Turner's CI check of every skill in context and the phrase 'using models to need them less' (keep the description canonical, regenerate the code).

articles.title: From me to you, in a link: a personal reading list, two briefs to build and use it, and the loop that makes it a day's work
articles.why: Background for the agents: personal reading lists in a link, a mechanism a personalised edition could use.

articles.title: A second reader the agent cannot skip: how two wrong emails became a gate on every draft
articles.why: Take the story: two emails went out wrong in the founder's voice, and the fix was a gate the agent cannot skip (deterministic checks, then a different model that fails closed). The old maker-checker idea applied to agents.

articles.title: A section for publishers: where to send someone new to this newsroom, and a site that keeps itself current
articles.why: Newsroom audience sections, site plumbing.

articles.title: A website to finish the book: gen-z-developers.sgit.ai, where the released book lives in the repository, the working book lives in a vault, and agents help me review it at every altitude
articles.why: Seeds the book's last part, how the edition was built (official versions in the repository, working versions in a vault, agents in roles), which Dinis wants a Gen Z developer to be able to do.

articles.title: Act as the job you want: if you are looking for a job, you have time, so do the work in public, make it linkable, and let the people who want to help you help you
articles.why: The core job-hunting chapter: if you are looking for a job you have time, so do the job in public, make it linkable, put your CV online, learn to publish with an agent first.

articles.title: Agency is not a yes: a scale for human and agent decisions, from rubber stamp to the reviewer who fixes the source
articles.why: Take the seven-level agency scale, from rubber stamp to the reviewer who fixes the source, and the line that below level 3 the person deciding carries the liability but has no real agency.

articles.title: Agent hooks in October 2026: a technical debrief on what each platform lets you see, stop and change, where hooks run, and where they fail
articles.why: Technical survey of hooks across ten coding agents; background for the agents writing the controls chapter, with the takeaway 'guardrails, not walls'.

articles.title: Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults: seven architectures from one agent to a swarm, a repository of recipes that gates sgit's releases, and what a hundred writers did to an append lane
articles.why: sgit multi-agent architecture recipes.

articles.title: Agentic cost is an engineering problem: a business plan for a service that reads the logs a company already has and finds the money, then the engineering
articles.why: Background for the agents: agentic cost as the price of skipping villager discipline. A business plan, not student costs.

articles.title: Agentics, ready to sell: what we showed at Agentic Engineering Live, who else is selling agentic services and at what price, the engagement path, and a marketplace for the consultants who deliver it
articles.why: Take the market facts: Gartner expects over 40% of agentic projects cancelled by end of 2027; boutiques sell £2,500 audits and €2,900 sprints; a marketplace of consultants is forming, a door for newcomers.

articles.title: An open AI governance framework, and what its licence let us build
articles.why: Background for the agents: twenty AI governance controls under CC BY-SA, turned into a graph. Too enterprise for the reader.

articles.title: Allowed is not right: an answer to Ashish Rajan's Northstar, with three policies and a twin you can run
articles.why: Take the Northstar example: the agent may refund up to $200, the customer is owed $120, it refunds $150, every control passes and the outcome is wrong.

articles.title: A locked-down desktop for an agent, by the minute, is still hard to rent
articles.why: agent desktop rental market survey

articles.title: Approve at altitude: decisions at every level, from strategy to one agent's step, where each level may narrow the one above and never widen it
articles.why: Decision-policy governance at enterprise scale; gives the agents the rule 'a lower level may narrow the one above, never widen it'.

articles.title: Are hooks the sweet spot? Moving an agent's rules from hope into hooks, rule by rule, until enforcement moves off the machine
articles.why: Take 'hope-based security' and the count: of the site's eleven agent rules only one was kept by something other than the agent; four moved fully into hooks.

articles.title: Attacks rewritten as mandates: 28 supply-chain incidents, the column each one was missing, and why the next maintainer is an agent
articles.why: Take 'reach beyond mandate' as the shape of every supply-chain attack (28 incidents) and the fact that the next maintainer holding a publish token is an agent (4,746 PRs in eight weeks).

articles.title: Authority outside the model: an answer to Satya Nadella on models as insider risks, principle by principle, with what we run, what we ship and what we plan
articles.why: Background for the agents: Nadella's seven principles mapped to the mandate. Enterprise framing, cited in map.json.

articles.title: Books from articles: why my books stall at 95%, why these articles do not, and a plan to turn them into books by Web Summit
articles.why: Books stall at 95% because they are one big batch; small finished pieces with a feedback loop ship; seeds both the publish chapter and the making-of.

articles.title: Brief the agent too: the people I talk to work with agents, so what I send has to reach both
articles.why: Take the story: a founder gave an article to their agent, which saw the team defending against states while its backups were undone and reset the target to T3. Readers now read through agents.

articles.title: Bringing my past work back: a daily worker that turns eighteen years of essays, talks, posts and tools into linkable articles, and why every team needs one
articles.why: Take the back-catalogue inventory (103 essays, 1,289 blog posts, 65 decks, 221 videos) and the point that work you cannot link is lost: talk to your future self.

articles.title: Case law for agents: principles from the top, precedent from the cases, and how a decision earns its way into code
articles.why: Precedent-driven decision policies; background on how a decision earns its way into code.

articles.title: Cedar and the policy vault: a debrief on the policy language agents are adopting, where our behaviour policies and sgit vaults meet it, and a brief for the MVP
articles.why: Cedar policy-language product brief.

articles.title: Chainguard, mapped: what it builds, what it publishes, how far up the stack its context goes, and where an open behaviour policy and an encrypted vault could plug in
articles.why: Company map, supply-chain specialist depth.

articles.title: A chat box on a site with no server, the plan, and the trade it makes
articles.why: Take the three honest tiers for a chat box with no server (a local matcher, a key in the reader's browser, a vault app with a bridge) and the fact that only one of them is free.

articles.title: Cloudflare as Lego blocks: what a non-specialist can build on it in October 2026, and an sgit vault in 83 lines
articles.why: The non-specialist's map of free cloud building blocks (static hosting, Workers 100,000 requests a day, R2, free models) assembled once with an agent; answers AWS and serverless outlines.

articles.title: Code review as a fractal semantic graph: source code is already one, and the review should read every layer of it
articles.why: Source code is already a fractal semantic graph, from stories down to the syntax tree; a refactor moves the bottom and leaves the top still. Map.json uses it for TDD and AST; it gives a newcomer a way to read code they did not write.

articles.title: Commander's intent is a behaviour policy: Sondera's argument in our words, the business layer above it, and five of our rules compiled to Cedar and tested
articles.why: Take 'agents do not go rogue; they follow instructions and fill the gaps' and commander's intent: write the objective and its limits together.

articles.title: Before you give an agent a connector, give the connector a twin
articles.why: Take the three questions to ask before connecting anything: what did the agent do, what did it see when it did it, and which actions can you undo. A twin of the connector (a journal plus a replay) answers all three.

articles.title: Custom UIs are not the exception: the inbox in 2026, where every message has its own universe
articles.why: Take the claim: a custom interface for each moment is now how interfaces get made, so building your own UI is normal, not exotic.

articles.title: Dark mode, and four more: five themes for the newsroom, chosen once and kept in your browser
articles.why: Newsroom theming implementation.

articles.title: Encrypted memory for agents that run somewhere else: sgit deployment patterns, from a Mac mini to Kubernetes
articles.why: Background for the agents: sgit deployment patterns, and the rule of one vault per trust boundary.

articles.title: Ephemeral town planner services: a better name than serverless, now that serverless includes things that bill you by the hour
articles.why: Explains serverless with Wardley's vocabulary and a test anyone can apply ('if it bills you by the hour when idle it is not serverless'); answers the Serverless and Micro-services outlines.

articles.title: Every link points back: 566 links between 105 articles, 15 that point forward, and why an article should know what came next and what corrected it
articles.why: Links point back in time (551 of 566); background for how the book's chapters should carry forward links and corrections.

articles.title: Every mistake added a rule: complexity, agents, and the way back to shipping
articles.why: The trap a new agent operator falls into: every mistake becomes a rule, the prompt grows, compaction comes sooner and new mistakes follow. The way out is small, tested, shipped components that no longer need a rule, plus short sessions. Speaks to the "when the agent is wrong" gap.

articles.title: Every risk is already accepted. The only question is by whom, and for how long.
articles.why: Take the quote: "Every risk is already accepted. The only question is by whom, and for how long."

articles.title: Explorer coding: a better name for what people call vibe coding, what it is good for, and the handover to villagers and town planners before anyone depends on it
articles.why: Defines explorer coding (what is called vibe coding) and the handover to villagers and town planners: the frame of the whole edition.

articles.title: Go slow to go fast: moving the newsroom from an explorer project to a villager one, with the brief to do it
articles.why: A worked handover with real numbers: about 2,700 lines of live reader code, 433 lines of tests the workflow never runs, two upstreams and no CSP; the fix is go slow to go fast, a pure refactor proved by identical bytes, then the explorer-to-villager phases. Fills the testing gap with a story.

articles.title: Firing journalists is the worst thing a publication can do: what a hiring decision says about where a publisher is going, and who to hire instead
articles.why: Take the line "what you measure is what you become" and the reading of hiring decisions as a statement of where an employer is going, a lens a job seeker can use on any company.

articles.title: Fix the page yourself: the bookmarklet trick from my security days, a page API every site should publish, and why the next user experience is the one the user customises, with six fixes running on this newsroom
articles.why: Take the bookmarklet story from a security assessment: the business owner liked the quick UI more than the exploit; the next UX is the one the user customises.

articles.title: Footprint and blast radius: what the agent actually did, and what it would have cost
articles.why: Adds "footprint" (what the agent actually did, read from the record and compared with the mandate) beside blast radius (what full use of a reach would cost, and whether there is a way back). Two words a newcomer can use about any agent they run.

articles.title: Four frameworks, one agent: iason's comparison of the OECD classification, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act, read against what runs here, with the evidence and the graphs
articles.why: AI risk framework comparison, governance depth.

articles.title: Free models, your own key: what a reader can use from the browser in October 2026, and what they cannot
articles.why: Practical map of what a newcomer can use free in October 2026 with their own key (Groq, Gemini AI Studio, Mistral, OpenRouter free models) and what changed.

articles.title: From a spreadsheet to a folder per person: how to run your contacts the way our agents do, with Google Drive, Gmail and the Claude app, before you touch a vault
articles.why: The most beginner-ready how-to in the newsroom: a Drive folder per person, a Claude Project connected to Drive and Gmail, a six-line policy (draft never send, append never rewrite, stay in the folder), a one-afternoon migration and five exercises. Fills the workspace gap with tools a student already has.

articles.title: From sending a file to sgit: eight months of SG/Send, told by its own briefs and commits, and how a file-sharing service became encrypted version control and vaults
articles.why: Take 'the technology worked; the use case was not there yet' ('users buy credits, test once, and don't come back') and the 22-minute feature; plus the record correcting memory.

articles.title: The future of news is the story vault, not the paywall
articles.why: news business model thesis

articles.title: Generation Z Developers (AI edition): the 2018 book that said act like you are part of the company, what it got right, and a new edition for the people I want to help
articles.why: The edition's plan (keep the name, frame with explorers/villagers/town planners, 90 of 138 files outlines); the founding brief for the writing agents.

articles.title: Going live with the reading meter: pay for what you read, go below zero if you like, and the numbers we will check in eight weeks
articles.why: reading meter launch hypotheses

articles.title: Green does not mean live
articles.why: "Shipped is a fact about the reader, not about your repository": a CI pass is not a release until you have checked what the user actually sees. Seeds the CI/testing section (a first-pass gap) and answers 2018 CI-Testing, SRE and devops.

articles.title: Handing secrets to agents and browsers: SG/Send's next focus, a key pair where the work runs, one-time drops, and a brief for a site that does only this
articles.why: Take the rule 'the secret goes from the drop into the tool, never into the chat', and that an agent told something is secret sometimes refuses to use it.

articles.title: Hired for the workflow: why October 2026 is the moment to get into agentic work, why you are more technical than you think, and how the edge starts with the application
articles.why: The thesis chapter: October 2026 is the moment; companies need AI operators not model builders; 71% of leaders prefer less experience with AI skills; PwC 62% wage premium; the edge starts with the application.

articles.title: Hooks are kernel code: a maturity model, the first ten hooks mapped, and a brief for a hooks site and feed where you pay for state, never to run
articles.why: Hooks maturity model and billing brief; gives agents 'treat a five-line hook like kernel code' and the three questions (power, trifecta legs, sandbox).

articles.title: Hope or enforcement: one customer service agent, three designs, and who keeps each promise
articles.why: Take the worked example: one customer-service agent in three designs (one broad model, a harness of tools, narrow agents behind a gateway), where most of the policy moves from hope to boundaries and the token cost falls.

articles.title: The human in the loop is a spectrum: how cheap it is to undo decides where a person belongs, and why the newsroom ships on its own while my email still waits for me
articles.why: One-way and two-way doors as the test for where a person belongs, with the newsroom shipping 14 releases a day on its own while email still waits; answers the 2018 one-way/two-way doors outline directly.

articles.title: How I work with Claude: one session per topic, agents with names, and memory you curate
articles.why: Six habits a beginner can copy on day one: one session per topic, named sessions with @names, an agent is a session with a role.md, memory is what the session reads and you curate it, vaults instead of broad permissions, a policy before every connector. Partly fills the "workspace from zero" gap.

articles.title: How much of this did I write? The numbers behind twenty articles in four weeks, and what the input actually was
articles.why: Hard numbers for the making-of part and for the opening frame: 63,000 words in (mostly 35 voice memos), 85,000 out through 122 releases, no article from a one-line prompt; corrections were about direction, not hallucination. "People with a direction are the input to the loop."

articles.title: The reader was always the product: a corrected history of how news got into this mess
articles.why: history of news economics

articles.title: How the newsletter is made: twenty-three articles, three issues, and every quote checked, written by the agent that makes it
articles.why: Take the method: read every source in full (72,000 words), the build checks quotes word for word, the agent checks what no gate can; and the honest backlog.

articles.title: How the voice works: why these articles sound like me, with a section in which Claude explains it from its side
articles.why: The voice is four inputs, not a setting: a corpus of 86 articles (51 from voice memos), the memos themselves, seven wording rules learned one correction at a time, and the author reading everything; includes a section in Claude's own words. For the newsroom chapter and the making-of.

articles.title: How to run synthetic users on your own site: five people who do not exist, a browser, and an afternoon
articles.why: A practical exercise a beginner can do in an afternoon: write five invented people with a situation and a question, let a model drive a real browser as each of them, then rate the findings and order them by cost. User testing without users, and a portfolio piece.

articles.title: I just want to buy the article: what happened when I tried to pay Harvard Business Review for one piece I wanted to answer, the arithmetic of a subscription, and ten things HBR could sell a reader like me, most of them already running on this newsroom
articles.why: Publisher micropayment economics.

articles.title: I miss it, so it is working: the people who decide the roadmap have to use the product, and the vault the newsroom now needs
articles.why: Take the rule that the people who decide the roadmap must use the product, and Dinis's admission that he failed this test with earlier startups. Direction from usage is the scarce part.

articles.title: If somebody built a company on code review: how I would do it, and why it is only now possible
articles.why: Background for the agents: graphs at every altitude, and code review as a science. Cited in map.json.

articles.title: Inside the Mesa Ranch desk: a page-by-page tour of an observation vault, from the cover to the knowledge graph you can play in time
articles.why: Walkthrough of a journalism vault demo.

articles.title: Inside the Northstar twin: thirteen refunds, four designs, and every decision played back
articles.why: Walkthrough of a deterministic refund twin; agents can borrow its cases ($261 split into three to fit the limit) as exercises.

articles.title: Fractal Semantic Graphs: everything connects to everything, and nobody has to share a schema
articles.why: The defining article for "fractal semantic graph" (the first pass took the term from knowledge-that-maintains-itself): everything is already a graph in its owner's vocabulary, and a short shared grammar, not a shared schema, links them. Answers 2018 graphs, DSL and DOT language.

articles.title: When journalism becomes intelligence, built: an observation desk for one data-center buildout, from an atlas of 78 events to a community impact tracker, in a vault you can open
articles.why: Take 'as AI makes content production easier, the advantage comes from how we observe the world' and the decision to make records synthetic rather than fake real ones.

articles.title: Judo for small countries: where Portugal, Romania and Estonia can add the most value in AI, and why the race for GPUs is not it
articles.why: For Portugal, Romania or Estonia the GPU race is a commodity layer only capital wins; the opportunity is the plumbing a talented person needs to sell a service to the world (company, cross-border hiring, payment, language, tax). Map.json uses it for civic responsibility; it also shows the young reader where demand will be.

articles.title: Knowing when to stop: what experience gives people, and what we have to design into agents
articles.why: Seniority is mostly knowing when to stop (who the attackers are, the phase of the business, the bottleneck, good enough), and agents lack it because their range is the feature. The newcomer's answer is constraints that carry perspective: a mandate, a named stop, narrow scope.

articles.title: Knowledge that maintains itself: semantic graphs for an organisation's policies and internal knowledge, briefing people and agents from the graph, and vaults to carry the brief
articles.why: Graphs as knowledge management: brief people and agents from a graph, not the pile; 'you do not have to get the graph right first, you have to maintain it'; answers the graphs outline.

articles.title: Liquid content needs water: liquefy the journalist's notebook, not the finished product
articles.why: newsroom workflow, journalism industry

articles.title: Memory is not a spectator sport: how a web of open sites, graphs and vaults became the memory for sessions like this one
articles.why: Memory for agents is context management: many context-specific memories, fractal so an agent loads only the altitude it needs, published and open, handed off through vaults, with provenance. Explains why your notes and published work matter to your future self.

articles.title: Move the cloud, not the code: twins, sovereignty that works in practice, and the migration that pays for itself on the day you switch
articles.why: Background for the agents: cloud twins and sovereignty in practice. Cited in map.json.

articles.title: My memory, checked: thinking out loud in a voice memo, publishing only what the record supports, and why peer review has moved to before publishing
articles.why: Think out loud, publish only what the record supports: 5 claims confirmed, 5 corrected, 2 not found; peer review has moved to before publishing; answers Facts and Talking to yourself.

articles.title: Twenty sites in fifteen days, and what that did to the writing
articles.why: Take the number: twenty sites in fifteen days, as a body of work split so each argument keeps its own history, with an index that starts from the reader's question.

articles.title: No server, by design: first I retired the database, now I am retiring the back end
articles.why: A beginner-sized architecture: first retire the database (files), then the back end (encrypted vaults keep the server blind, the app runs in the browser, only commodity products are left on the server), and write down the gaps you accept. Answers 2018 serverless, Hugo and micro-services.

articles.title: Not a straight line: working for RiskMandate by working on the newsroom, and why the thinking is never wasted
articles.why: Take the story: the newsroom solved in two days a vault problem that six months of RiskMandate work had not, and "the thinking is never wasted when it is written down and open source" (the paused Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds).

articles.title: Omnichannel programming: briefs by voice, reviews by voice, previews on the phone, and one shared state underneath, at every stage from explorer to town planner
articles.why: How a new generation programs: brief by voice, review by voice, preview on the phone, one shared state (git, vaults, briefs, graphs); 54 messages in, 40 releases out in three days.

articles.title: On the record: signed opinions from experts, paid when readers value them, and a share for the people whose ideas an article uses
articles.why: Take the research point that real names did not make comments better, stable identities did, and signed, withdrawable professional opinions as the alternative to comments.

articles.title: One article, five readers: a librarian, a cartographer, a historian, an explainer and a storyteller read the same piece
articles.why: Background for the agents: the Librarian, Cartographer, Historian, Explainer and Storyteller roles, which can be reused to produce the book.

articles.title: One vault, ten agents, 35,000 objects: what sgit does when the repository is big and the clients are many, measured on the vault behind this newsroom
articles.why: sgit performance measurements.

articles.title: Open source is not free: who pays to keep the long tail working?
articles.why: Take the numbers: 6.99% of Homebrew macOS installs in 30 days (16.66% in a year) are on versions older than the newest three; a 20p card fee dominates any payment under about five pounds.

articles.title: Our first PR in Ruflo: an ABP-governed SGit page, merged into ruvnet/ruflo, and the four pieces that got it there
articles.why: Take the first-contribution story: a one-file, 83-line documentation PR merged into a 9,625-commit project because it was exact about what it did not claim.

articles.title: Pay after you read: how a reading meter became a working business model in one afternoon, one release at a time
articles.why: Take the number: a working pay-on-demand publication in seven releases in 3 hours 40 minutes. This is the meter the book's reader uses, and an example of small releases that each grow from using the last one.

articles.title: Pay to keep your persona: readers should pay because it helps them, not because they feel they should
articles.why: reader persona pricing argument

articles.title: Paying after the value: why a balance that can go negative feels different from a subscription, the psychology behind it, and the experiment this newsroom is running
articles.why: Take the gym figure ($17 a visit when $10 was available) and pay-after-the-value as a business-model idea a young founder can test cheaply.

articles.title: Places of highest leverage: where to focus when the agents can go in every direction, told with three days of real steps
articles.why: When agents can build in any direction, direction is the scarce part: work where the next step moves the needle most and nothing blocks you; start without knowing the end; ship and use each step; walking back and parking are not failure. This is advice for a newcomer, and map.json does not cite it.

articles.title: Policy as code needs a policy first: what an agent behaviour policy adds, and how to reverse engineer one from the code, the spreadsheet or the paper you already have
articles.why: Policy as code versus behaviour policy; gives agents 'a rule the agent can rewrite is a setting, not a control'.

articles.title: A web application security challenge to Portugal, 2010: my IBWAS keynote in Lisbon, slide by slide, with what came true, what I got wrong and what still stands
articles.why: Take what came true in 16 years (liability, disclosure, HTTPS) and the lesson that regulation, not fear, moved governments; answers Stories to tell and Civic responsibility.

articles.title: Hacking Portugal, 2016: my BSidesLisbon keynote and the book that stopped at 95%, slide by slide, with what holds ten years later and what a new edition needs
articles.why: Take 'to hack means to solve problems', the Portuguese Hacking Service for 15 to 21 year olds, and that agents make a small country leading in code more possible.

articles.title: GenAI in Portuguese, 2024: my OWASP Global AppSec talk in Lisbon, the first public demo of The Cyber Boardroom, slide by slide, with what two years of agents have confirmed and changed
articles.why: Take the quiz: the sixth most powerful programming language is Portuguese, because prompts are natural language; your own language is now a programming language.

articles.title: Portugal and Europe, 2025: five essays on Portuguese as a programming language, an open-source sovereign cloud, regulation as graphs and Europe's chance in GenAI, and how they read a year and a half later
articles.why: Sovereignty and regulation as graphs; background for a civic-responsibility then-now, with 'sovereignty is the ability to move'.

articles.title: Price it, then give it away: the early access programme as the next step after "do they miss it"
articles.why: Take the move: a price says what you think something is worth; giving it away at that price to people who know you is the cleanest test of whether you are right.

articles.title: The proof is two clicks behind the claim, what the homepage gets wrong, and the fix
articles.why: sgit homepage critique

articles.title: The proof moved up, the homepage after the rebuild, next to the before pictures
articles.why: sgit homepage rebuild notes

articles.title: Re-anchoring: keeping an agent's rules alive through every summary, and a canary that shows when they are not
articles.why: Take the number: this site's session was summarised 18 times in a month, keeping about 1.7% each time. Rules have to be re-read from a file after each summary (a SessionStart hook), not remembered.

articles.title: Replicating the agentic inbox: a walkthrough from one Claude session to a team of agents that never press send
articles.why: The how-to the first pass could not find: one Claude session, then roles that talk in files, the agent gets its own Workspace mailbox and its own Claude seat, every email a draft a person sends. Seeds the workspace chapter and the concept "drafts, never send".

articles.title: Research, delivered as a vault: what companies that sell research could do with fractal graphs, behaviour policies for AI-enabled products, and evaluations run by a governed agent hive

concepts.definition: What someone builds for themselves says what they actually want, in a form that runs, better than any requirements document.
Dinis's term for the people companies need now: not model builders but people who use the tools and workflows to get things done.

Being hired for the ability to run agentic workflows, as people were once hired for breaking apps or building websites, degree or no degree; the edge shows when candidates look equal, starting with the application.

concepts.term: act as the job you want
concepts.definition: If you are looking for a job you have time: do the job before you have it, in public, so it can be linked: reach does not matter, the link lets the people who want to help you forward it.
A personal publishing loop: voice memo in, an agent researches, checks and writes in your voice, a validated static site out, readers pay a little if it is useful.

Programming across voice, chat, phone, IDE and pull requests where every channel reads and writes one shared state (git, vaults, briefs, graphs), as against multichannel, where each keeps its own copy.
A written request an agent session can start from: what is asked, what exists, what remains; the unit of work between a person and agents.
Amazon's test, used here for agents: a two-way door can be undone cheaply (a page correction), a one-way door cannot (a sent email); the cost of undoing decides where a person belongs.

What an output or a row of an agent's reach would cost if it went wrong in full today; put the person where it is large and the output cannot be undone (defined fully in footprint-and-blast-radius, outside the surveyed set).
For one agent in one deployment: what it can reach, what it was authorised to do, the gap between the two, and what actually stands in the way of each capability.
Mandate is what the agent (or credential) is for; reach is everything it can touch; the gap between them is the risk, and every supply-chain attack used it.
Rules written in a prompt and kept only if the model keeps them: better than nothing, not enough on its own.
Small programs the agent's harness runs at fixed points (before and after a tool call, on prompt, on stop) that can see, block or rewrite actions; guardrails, not walls.
Behaviour says what an agent may do, decision says who chooses at a branch point and on what evidence, workflow says in what order.
Every control can pass and the outcome still be wrong (a $150 refund where $120 was owed); proving the right outcome needs a written definition of right.
Simon Willison's term the newsroom uses: private data, untrusted content and a way out in one agent or skill; any agent with all three needs a control even if honest.

What was actually done, kept outside anyone's memory (commits, briefs, transcripts, versions); 'the record catches up with the instinct', so thinking out loud becomes safe, and peer review moves to before publishing (confirmed, corrected or not found).
Every review is a file written once against published criteria, and every finding is answered: fixed in which version, declined and why, or open.
An agent's own logs and account of itself; evidence written outside the agent is more honest and still needs reading.

concepts.term: code is a liability / minimal viable code path
concepts.definition: Every shipped line is a capability someone may misuse; the future is the smallest code that does exactly the job, made safe by model-built tests and maps.
A better name for serverless: scales to zero, costs nothing idle, starts fast, a commodity exposed for others; test: if it bills you by the hour when idle, it is not serverless.
Knowledge held as a graph with an ontology and taxonomy per element, each part in its own vocabulary, every node openable as a graph of its own; briefs come from the slice you need.
In open source anyone can fork, which protects founders, customers and investors from each other; forks take hold only when someone stops executing.
The subject buys the first line, the first line buys the paragraph, the paragraph buys the email: open with the short answer in plain text.
Me alone, me through an agent, an agent in its own voice; every byline should say which.
Using a model provider with your own API key called straight from the browser, so nobody else holds the key or pays for your questions.

A graph with context in two directions: a value chain anchored on a user and a need, and an evolution axis (usually genesis, custom built, product, commodity, though the axis is a choice). Read out like a story, it says what to build, what to buy, and where a market exists. Every node is itself a map.

Where the most value can be added now, nothing blocks you, and you can start without knowing how the whole problem ends. It is not where the biggest problem is. Each step is shipped and used before the next is chosen.
Agents can build in any direction; what they cannot generate is the sense of what to build next and when to stop. People with a direction are the input to the loop, not displaced by it.

The judgement that experience gives people (who the attackers are, the phase of the business, the bottleneck, what good enough looks like). Agents lack it by design, so it has to be supplied as constraints: a mandate, a stop named in advance, a narrow scope.
What the agent actually did, read afterwards from the record and compared with its mandate. It is the partner of blast radius, which is what a reach would cost if used in full.
Shipped is a fact about the reader, not about your repository: a release has to check the boundary the user is on, not only the ones CI can see.

concepts.term: an agent is a session with a focus
concepts.definition: An agent is a named session (an @name) that reads a few documents about the project and a role.md saying what it does and does not do. One session per topic, never mixed threads.
The rule for an agentic inbox: agents read, label and draft, and a person reads, edits and presses send. The agent has its own mailbox and its own Claude seat, never yours.

concepts.term: threat ladder (draw the line where the attacker is)
concepts.definition: Security starts from who the threat agent is, the attack vector and how sophisticated it is. On a ladder from your own mistakes up to states, plan to the rung that matches what you protect, do the basics consistently, and write down what you accept above that rung.
Every risk an organisation has is already accepted by somebody, so the questions are who accepted it and until when.
Agents in loops make real decisions, but responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate, because the grant is the moment of authorisation.

Seven levels from rubber stamp to the reviewer who fixes the source. A decision is capped by its weakest ingredient (options, context, time, incentives, escalation, authority). Below level 3 the person deciding carries liability without agency.

The complexity trap for agent operators: each mistake becomes a rule, the prompt grows, compaction comes sooner and new mistakes follow. The way out is small, tested, shipped components that move right on the map and no longer need the rule.
Keeping an agent's rules in a file that a hook prints back after every summary, so the rules are restored rather than remembered, with a canary that shows they are still being read.

Invented people, each with a situation, a question, what they know and what makes them leave, played by a model that drives a real browser one screenshot at a time, so it can get lost as a person would.
The explorer-to-villager move done as a pure refactor, proved by the live site serving the same bytes, before adding tests and hardening.

Retire the database (files), then the back end: encrypted vaults keep the server blind, the app runs in the browser, only commodity products are left on the server, and the gaps you accept are written down.
The startup test: if users would miss the product when it is gone, it is working. The people who set the roadmap have to use the product themselves.

concepts.term: open source means nobody can lock you in
concepts.definition: Open source is a copyright licence granting copying, use and change. Its real power is that nobody can lock you in. Security depends on whether somebody had the time and money to review the code.
AI is available to incumbents and newcomers alike, so the outcome is decided by where each sits on the evolution axis and how much past success it has to protect.

gaps: Setting up your workspace from zero: a Google Workspace (or equivalent), GitHub account, Claude/ChatGPT connected to it, and the agentic email workflow; short-punchy-and-co-written asks for this chapter and no surveyed article is a how-to (replicating-the-agentic-inbox exists only outside the surveyed set).

Learning how to learn with an agent: how to use agents to understand rather than skip understanding (reading code you did not write, asking why), for someone with no prior coding; the 2018 Learning chapter has no article behind it beyond hired-for-the-workflow.
Fear, impostor syndrome and anxiety about AI among young people: the map notes 'fear of AI among young Europeans'; two-years-in-the-opposite is Dinis's story, not advice for a newcomer.

The job hunt mechanics in 2026: interviews, take-home tests done with or without AI, what a junior/entry role actually looks like day to day, freelancing and Upwork; agentics-ready-to-sell covers consultancy, not first jobs.
Testing and TDD as what lets an agent change code safely, for a beginner (the map points to code-review-as-a-fractal-semantic-graph, outside the surveyed set).
The command line, Linux and git basics as practical skills (sgit-is-a-standard argues git's design, not how to use it).
Debugging and reading errors with an agent; when the agent is wrong and how you notice.
Costs and money for a newcomer: what a Claude/ChatGPT plan, tokens and free tiers cost a student (the-tokens-hook and free-models-your-own-key are partial).
Privacy, data protection and ethics for someone building with agents (GDPR outline has no newsroom article in scope).
Habits, focus, the zone and burnout (Power of Habits, The Zone, Start with Why, Dopamine outlines have nothing).
Mentors and community: finding people to learn from, meetups, OWASP chapters today (only act-as-the-job-you-want touches it).
Diversity and accessibility of the field: who gets in now that the bar is lower (Why diversity matters outline; fix-the-page-yourself touches accessibility only).
Maths and fundamentals (Love Maths, Assembly and Bytecode, Pointers, Strings should be banned): whether a newcomer still needs them, and why.
Hardware and making (Raspberry Pi, IoT, Minecraft outlines): no article; the editor may cut them.

Covered with stories and numbers. A first red-green test written for a beginner is still not covered.

Covers noticing and containing agent mistakes. Reading a stack trace with an agent is not covered.

Learning how to learn with an agent: partly by how-i-work-with-claude, code-review-as-a-fractal-semantic-graph, memory-is-not-a-spectator-sport, how-much-of-this-did-i-write. Curated memory, reading code by its layers, and direction as the input. There is still no beginner exercise in "ask why".
